transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-02-28
Time: 15:00 PT
Duration: 52 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Jordan Blake (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Evan Park (StratifyAI Head of Search), Maya Lopez (ML Eng Manager), Tom Reynolds (CTO), Alex Chen (SRE)

Summary:
StratifyAI is evaluating Redwood for embeddings-based search + reranking across a product search and recommendations use case. They run a hybrid search today (BM25 + vector) using Milvus for vectors; looking at latency targets (~50-150ms for top-k), peak QPS ~250, average ~60. Key concerns: index dimensionality (1536 vs 768), vector DB choice and hosting (hosted Pinecone vs self-hosted Milvus), throughput and batching, secure VPC/private deployment, SOC2/KMS, and cost tradeoffs between Redwood Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private.

Topics:
- Current architecture and constraints
- Embedding dimensionality and model choice
- Vector DB integrations and ANN indexes (HNSW / IVF+PQ)
- Throughput, latency SLOs, batching and KV cache implications
- Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private deployment tradeoffs
- Security/compliance (SOC2, KMS, VPC peering)

Action items (captured in metadata): see action_items field above

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, um we wanted to start by understanding your current stack and goals for embeddings and reranking. Evan, do you want to kick off?
[00:15] Evan (StratifyAI): Yeah thanks, uh quick background: we power product search and a recommendations widget, we've been hybrid for a year, baseline retrieval is BM25 then we do vector rerank. Right now vectors in Milvus, dimensions 1536 from a text-embedding-3 like model, but we're exploring denser 768 vectors to save cost and reduce latency.
[00:35] Maya: our peak query load is about 250 QPS but that's bursty, daily average closer to 60. Top-k is typically k=10, we care about P@10 and latency at the tail.
[00:50] Priya (Redwood SE): Great, are you doing end-to-end rerank in a single request or multi-stage? how much of the scoring is neural vs traditional signals?
[01:05] Evan: Multi-stage — BM25 first stage gives 100 results, then we embed and do ANN to get 50, then rerank with a small transformer that uses embeddings + metadata. Neural rerank is heavy but only on top candidates.
[01:20] Alex (SRE): infra-wise, Milvus is hosted in our AWS account on EC2, using HNSW. We're seeing index memory pressure at the 1.2B vector scale and also cost on storage.
[01:35] Jordan: okay, thanks. From Redwood's side two things to consider: model dimensionality and index structure will drive both latency and cost, and the deployment mode (Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private) will determine network topology and data residency.
[01:50] Tom (CTO): We are sensitive to PII, so we'd need SOC2 controls and KMS for keys. Also VPC peering is a hard requirement for Private mode.
[02:05] Priya: Understood. Quick Q: do you have any SLAs today or target latency percentiles for the app?
[02:15] Maya: target p95 end-to-end for top-k is ~150ms, ideally below 100ms for simple queries. For heavy rerank queries we can tolerate up to 300ms but prefer under 200.
[02:30] Priya: got it. For those numbers we typically recommend a combination of: a) smaller dim embeddings if they preserve quality, b) tuned HNSW or IVF PQ for high-recall first pass, c) Redwood batching + KV prefix cache to reduce repeated token compute on hosted generation/rerank.
[02:50] Evan: can you explain the KV cache comment? we don't do generation, just embeddings and rerank models.
[02:58] Priya: yeah sorry, mixing notes — KV cache is more for decoder LM workloads; for you relevant parts are caching embeddings for frequently requested docs and caching rerank results for repeated queries. Redwood's platform supports prefix caching and can store top-K embedding vectors in a fast cache to avoid re-embedding hot docs.
[03:15] Jordan: also note that with Dedicated you get reserved GPU pools that help with predictable throughput for rerank models, whereas Hosted gives you the fastest time-to-value but less isolation. Private gives you full control if you need on-prem or strict VPC-only network paths.
[03:35] Evan: we're trying to weigh Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private. if we do Hosted, can we keep vectors in our Milvus and call Redwood for rerank? or do you want vectors in Redwood?
[03:50] Priya: You can keep vectors in your DB and call Redwood for embedding generation and rerank — that's a common pattern. For lowest latency, colocating vectors (i.e., using Redwood-managed vector storage in the same region or Dedicated cluster) reduces cross-service hops. Important is network latency between your Milvus and Redwood endpoints — if in same cloud region and VPC peering set up, it's fine.
[04:10] Alex: VPC peering is something we can do, we just need the network diagrams and firewall rules.
[04:20] Jordan: we'll share our standard network diagram and SOC2 pack as next steps.
[04:28] Maya: back to dimensionality — we tried reducing to 768 and saw a small drop in R@10 but big savings in memory. How do you typically recommend choosing dims?
[04:40] Priya: run targeted A/B on your core queries: 1536 vs 1024 vs 768 with the same ANN config. Often model choice (embedding model) matters more than raw dim; sometimes smaller dims with a retrained projection preserve most signal. We'll share a benchmark template for that.
[05:00] Evan: do you have priors — like at 768 what drop we should expect?
[05:07] Priya: depends on data distribution; ballpark maybe 1-5% drop in recall, but some difficult queries degrade more. That's why the benchmark spreadsheet will help.
[05:20] Tom: about ANN options — we've been on HNSW but worried about memory. What about IVF+PQ to trade memory for slightly higher latency?
[05:35] Priya: IVF+PQ is a good memory/cost tradeoff at large scale. HNSW gives excellent recall and fast query latency but needs more RAM. IVF+PQ with quantization reduces index size; query latency increases but with appropriate shards and hardware it can meet your SLOs. We can share recommended HNSW parameters (efConstruction, efSearch) and PQ settings for your volumes.
[05:55] Evan: throughput — can Redwood handle 250 peak QPS for rerank? our rerank model is a 200M parameter transformer running on GPU.
[06:10] Jordan: yes — for that workload we typically recommend Dedicated for predictable throughput if rerank is GPU-bound. With Dedicated you can reserve GPU pools and add autoscaling rules; with Hosted you may see variable wait times at peak. For 250 QPS of the 200M model you might need multiple concurrent replicas and batching.
[06:30] Priya: also consider asynchronous rerank for non-latency-critical queries — fetch top candidates, return quickly, and rerank in the background for eventual improvement. But for the main product search path where latency matters, Dedicated + batching + quantization for model weights can reduce per-request GPU time.
[06:55] Alex: on Dedicated, what about isolation and data persistence? we want index snapshots and audit logs.
[07:05] Priya: Dedicated gives you customer-dedicated GPU pools and data isolation by default; snapshots and audit logs are supported, and you can route logs to your SIEM. Private deployment gives you even more control — you host the runtime in your VPC or on-prem, and Redwood control plane can be optional. That satisfies strict compliance.
[07:25] Tom: cost — can you ballpark cost difference between Hosted vs Dedicated?
[07:33] Jordan: Hosted is OPEX with per-embedding/per-rerank token or request pricing; Dedicated is typically commit-based with lower unit costs at scale. We'll send a pricing sheet with examples tailored to your 250 QPS and index size.
[07:45] Maya: security — we need SAML SSO, RBAC, KMS integration, and SOC2 type II evidence.
[07:55] Jordan: Redwood supports SSO via SAML/OIDC, RBAC in Console, KMS/backed keys, and we can share SOC2 artifacts. For Private we can also integrate with your HSM if needed.
[08:08] Evan: what's the easiest path to validate end-to-end? we want to run a PoC that measures recall, latency, and cost.
[08:18] Priya: common approach: we run a 2–4 week PoC. Step 1, you run our benchmark template on a sample corpus with your current stack; Step 2, we provision Redwood Hosted trial (or Dedicated sandbox) and run same queries against Redwood-managed embedding model + index, and also test hybrid with your Milvus (colocated). We'll compare recall, latency p50/p95/p99 and cost per query.
[08:43] Alex: for Milvus integration, do you have connectors or do we push vectors to Redwood?
[08:50] Priya: we have integrations and recommended patterns — push embeddings to your DB and call Redwood for embedding generation/rerank, or push vectors into Redwood's managed index for lower latency. We also have a connector pattern for Milvus and can share a short integration guide.
[09:05] Evan: what about versioning and rollouts? we do frequent model changes and need canaries.
[09:12] Jordan: Redwood supports model version pinning and canary rollouts; you can route a percentage of traffic to new model variants and monitor quality regressions. Console has per-model dashboards and you can set alerts tied to prompt sets / evals.
[09:28] Tom: any limits on dimensionality or embeddings size?
[09:34] Priya: no hard limits, but larger dims increase RAM and storage. For Dedicated/Private you can select hardware with more memory. We typically recommend profiling sample index size: vectors * dim * 4 bytes (float32) plus index overhead. For 100M vectors at 1536 dims that grows quickly.
[09:54] Evan: can you show a quick calc? we're at ~30M docs, average vector 1536, storing HNSW — what's rough memory?
[10:05] Priya: rough calc: 30M * 1536 * 4 bytes ~ 184 GB raw for vectors; HNSW overhead could double to 350–400 GB depending on connectivity. So it's significant. Moving to PQ can reduce by 4–8x.
[10:25] Maya: that matches our ops numbers. Good to have a concrete calc in the benchmark template.
[10:33] Jordan: we'll include that.
[10:38] Evan: about hybrid search — currently we BM25 then vector; any recommendations for combining scores?
[10:45] Priya: normalize both signals and use a learned weights approach if you have labeled data. Another simple pattern: weighted sum with online tuning per query class. For rerank, using a small neural model that accepts both sparse + dense features often yields best ranking improvements.
[11:00] Alex: we have some labeled clicks for top results; would that help for a learned combiner?
[11:06] Maya: yes, we have logs we could label.
[11:10] Priya: perfect — for PoC, include a small labeled eval set so we can measure learned combiner improvements.
[11:18] Jordan: any blockers for starting a PoC?
[11:22] Tom: legal / procurement need contract clauses for data handling, but that's normal. Security will want SOC2 docs and a network diagram.
[11:32] Jordan: we'll send security pack and a standard MSA + data addendum.
[11:36] Evan: on performance, do you have guidance for batching rerank requests? we want to minimize GPU utilization without increasing tail latency.
[11:44] Priya: batching is key — group reranks where possible; Redwood's serving runtime supports dynamic batching with latency SLOs — you can set max batch size and max wait. For 250 QPS and small model you can batch 8–16 in-flight requests to improve utilization while keeping p95 targets. We can help pick batch knobs during the PoC.
[12:05] Maya: curious about concurrency planning — how many GPU replicas for 200M model to hit 250 QPS at p95 150ms?
[12:15] Priya: approximate — if a single optimized replica handles ~30 QPS at target latency with batching and quantized weights, you'd need ~9 replicas; Dedicated lets you reserve those. We'll run microbenchmarks in PoC to refine.
[12:30] Evan: what about quantization — does Redwood support int8 or 4-bit?
[12:36] Priya: yes, we support several quantization profiles. 4-bit / int8 quantization reduces memory and can keep latency lower; quality impacts depend on model. For rerank transformer usually int8 is safe; we can surface recommended profiles per model.
[12:50] Jordan: switching briefly to costs on storage — if we host vectors in Redwood, can we set retention tiers?
[12:58] Priya: yep you can tier cold storage vs hot index. Hot index for HNSW, cold for archived vectors. Console can show token/cost breakdown per route.
[13:10] Alex: on compliance, do you offer customer-managed keys?
[13:14] Jordan: yes KMS/HSM integrations and customer-managed keys are available in Dedicated and Private offerings.
[13:22] Maya: any red flags with our plan to move to 768 dims if we keep model quality?
[13:30] Priya: only if you see query classes that rely on fine-grained distinctions; that's why evaluation per-query-class is important. Generally 768 is a good tradeoff for many product catalogs.
[13:44] Evan: timeline — if we start PoC in early March, what are realistic milestones?
[13:50] Jordan: Week 0: baseline capture with your current infra (you run benchmark spreadsheet). Week 1–2: Redwood runs hosted/Dedicated runs on sample corpus. Week 3: joint analysis and model/dim tuning. Week 4: decision and next steps (pilot contract or extended PoC).
[14:08] Tom: procurement — we'll need pricing scenarios for Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private.
[14:14] Jordan: understood — I'll include three scenarios in the pricing sheet.
[14:19] Evan: any integrations for search stack observability? we want traces from query to rerank and cost per query.
[14:25] Priya: Console has per-route per-model breakdowns, tracing hooks, and you can export traces/logs to your observability backend. We can instrument top-k latency and cost attribution.
[14:40] Maya: okay let's talk Milvus connector specifics, can we get a short doc?
[14:45] Priya: yes, we'll share a Milvus connector doc — pattern: either push embeddings to Redwood index (best latency) or keep in Milvus and call Redwood rerank; for latter we recommend colocating services in same region plus VPC peering.
[14:58] Alex: we use autoscaling groups with Milvus nodes, any recommended node sizes?
[15:05] Priya: depends on index size; we'll propose EC2 instance types with high memory for HNSW and CPU-optimized for IVF PQ background tasks.
[15:18] Evan: competition — we evaluated Pinecone but saw higher cost at scale and limited control.
[15:25] Jordan: Pinecone is common alternative; Redwood differentiator is unified runtime and ability to run Dedicated/Private for more control.
[15:35] Tom: any privacy caveats if we send vectors to Redwood Hosted?
[15:40] Jordan: data in Hosted is encrypted at rest and in transit, but for strict privacy we'd recommend Dedicated or Private where you can control key management.
[15:50] Maya: okay, sounds good.
[15:55] Jordan: quick recap: we'll send benchmark template, pricing scenarios, SOC2 pack, Milvus connector, and suggested HNSW/PQ parameters. Priya will draft technical guide and params.
[16:08] Evan: thanks — we'll prepare sample corpus and run baseline metric capture by Mar 1.
[16:15] Jordan: great. We'll schedule a follow-up SE deep dive week of Mar 7.
[16:20] Tom: one more question — can Redwood run on-prem for us later?
[16:25] Priya: yes Private on-prem is supported, though it takes more lead time for installation and networking, typically 4–8 weeks depending on environment.
[16:35] Alex: will SRE be invited to the deep dive?
[16:38] Jordan: yes we'll loop in infra and invite SRE.
[16:41] Maya: thanks everyone.
[16:44] Jordan: thanks all — action items and next steps captured and we'll follow up with the docs.
[16:50] [call ends — rough timestamps continue, meeting lasted ~52 minutes]
